Every shape is there, from Jupiter to Judy, if the imagination chooses to find it. The poorer, less favored relations thought Peter would probably remember them at the end precisely because he had done nothing for them while alive. Jonah argued that men liked their wills to surprise people. Martha said nobody ought to be surprised if he left most of his money to those least expecting it. Besides, surely a brother lying there with his legs swollen by dropsy must begin to feel that blood was thicker than water. Even if he did not change his will, he might have cash by him. At all events, some genuine relations ought to be on the premises, watching those who scarcely counted as relatives at all. Wills had been forged and contested before; such proceedings seemed to hold the golden, misty advantage of somehow supporting people who had been left nothing. And unrelated people might be caught carrying things off, with poor Peter helpless in bed! Someone ought to keep watch. On that point Solomon and Jane agreed with them. Various nephews, nieces, and cousins, reasoning still more subtly about the possible whims of a man free to will his property away however he pleased, felt generously that the family interest needed defending. Visiting Stone Court would only be right. Martha, now Mrs. Cranch, lived in the Chalky Flats and suffered from wheezing, so she could not make the journey. But her son, poor Peter’s own nephew, could represent her to advantage and keep Uncle Jonah from taking an unfair share of whatever unlikely events might occur. In short, the Featherstone blood carried a general conviction that everyone must watch everyone else, and that everyone else would do well to remember the Almighty was watching too.

Relations were therefore constantly arriving at Stone Court or leaving it. Mary Garth had the unpleasant job of taking their messages upstairs to Mr. Featherstone, who refused to see any of them, and the still more unpleasant job of returning with that answer. As housekeeper, she felt obliged by local hospitality to invite them to stay for a meal. But with Mr. Featherstone bedridden, she decided to consult Mrs. Vincy about the additional food being consumed downstairs.

“Oh, darling, when there’s property and someone’s dying, you must be generous. Heaven knows I don’t begrudge them every ham in the house—just keep the best for the funeral. Always have some stuffed veal ready, and a good cheese cut open. You have to expect an open house at a time like this,” said the hospitable Mrs. Vincy, whose cheerful voice and bright plumage had returned.

Some callers, however, arrived and stayed even after generous helpings of veal and ham. Brother Jonah was one. Most families contain such disagreeable members; perhaps the highest aristocracy has gigantic versions, with colossal debts and bloating purchased at greater expense. Jonah had come down in the world and chiefly supported himself by an occupation he modestly avoided boasting of, though it was much better than swindling on the stock exchange or the racecourse. It did not require him to remain in Brassing as long as he had a comfortable corner and plenty to eat elsewhere. He chose the kitchen corner, partly from preference and partly to avoid Solomon, of whom he held a strongly brotherly opinion. Sitting in an excellent armchair in his best suit, with good food always in sight, he enjoyed the comforting certainty of being on the premises, mingled with passing associations of Sunday and the bar at the Green Man. He informed Mary that he would remain within reach of Peter as long as the poor fellow was above ground. A family’s troublesome members are generally either its wits or its fools. Jonah was the Featherstones’ wit. He joked with the maids when they approached the fire, but treated Miss Garth as a suspicious person and followed her with a cold stare.

One pair of eyes would have been fairly easy for Mary to endure. Unfortunately, young Cranch had traveled all the way from the Chalky Flats to represent his mother and keep watch on Uncle Jonah. He too felt duty-bound to remain, chiefly in the kitchen, keeping his uncle company. Young Cranch did not stand exactly midway between wit and fool: he leaned a little toward the latter. His squint left his feelings uncertain, except that they were plainly not forceful. When Mary entered and Jonah’s cold, investigating eyes followed her, young Cranch turned the same way and seemed determined that she should notice his squint. It was as if he were doing it deliberately, like the gypsies when Borrow read the New Testament to them. This was a little too much for poor Mary. Sometimes it made her feel sick; sometimes she could hardly keep a straight face. Finding an opportunity one day, she could not resist describing the kitchen scene to Fred. Nothing would stop him going straight to see it, pretending merely to pass through. But the moment those four eyes faced him, he had to rush out through the nearest door, which led to the dairy. There, beneath the high roof among the milk pans, he gave way to laughter that echoed hollowly and could be heard perfectly in the kitchen. He escaped through another door. Jonah, who had not previously seen Fred’s pale complexion, long legs, and delicate, drawn face, prepared a store of sarcasms ingeniously combining these features with the lowest moral failings.

“Well, Tom, your trousers aren’t nearly so gentlemanly, are they? And your legs aren’t half so fine and long,” Jonah told his nephew, winking to suggest that these undeniable observations contained a deeper meaning. Tom looked down at his legs, without making clear whether he preferred his moral superiority to a more sinful length of limb and a disreputably refined pair of trousers.

There were watchful eyes in the large paneled parlor too, and close relatives eager to sit up through the night. Many people came, ate lunch, and went away. But Solomon and the lady who had been Jane Featherstone for twenty-five years before becoming Mrs. Waule found it worthwhile to stay for hours every day. Their only identifiable occupation was observing the crafty Mary Garth—so cunning that nothing could be detected against her—and producing occasional dry, wrinkled signs of tears over their exclusion from their brother’s room. These hinted at torrents possible in a wetter season. As the old man lost the strength to amuse himself with cutting remarks to his family, his dislike of them seemed to increase. Too weak to sting, he had all the more poison flowing back through his veins.

Distrusting Mary’s message, they had presented themselves together in the bedroom doorway. Both wore black. Mrs. Waule held a partly unfolded white handkerchief, and both faces were a sort of half-mourning purple. Meanwhile Mrs. Vincy, her cheeks pink and her pink ribbons fluttering, was actually giving their own brother a cordial. Pale Fred, with short curls such as one would naturally expect on a gambler, lounged comfortably in a large chair.

As soon as Featherstone saw these funeral figures appearing against his orders, anger strengthened him more effectively than the cordial. He lay supported by a bedrest, his gold-headed walking stick always beside him. Seizing it, he swept it back and forth as widely as his strength allowed, as though driving off hideous apparitions, and cried out in a hoarse shriek:
“Stay back, Mrs. Waule! Back, Solomon!”

“Oh, Brother Peter,” Mrs. Waule began, but Solomon raised a restraining hand. Nearly seventy, with broad cheeks and small, evasive eyes, he was far smoother-tempered than Peter and considered himself considerably shrewder. He was indeed unlikely to be deceived by anyone, since people could hardly be greedier or more dishonest than he already suspected. Even the unseen powers, he thought, might be soothed by an occasional gentle acknowledgment from a man of property who could have been as irreligious as other men.
“Brother Peter,” he said in a coaxing but solemnly official voice, “it’s only right that I speak to you about the Three Crofts and the Manganese. The Almighty knows what’s weighing on my mind—”

“Then he knows more than I care to,” Peter answered. He lowered his stick in a gesture of truce that also carried a threat: he turned it around so the gold head could serve as a club at close quarters, and stared at Solomon’s bald scalp.

“You may regret some things if you don’t talk to me, Brother,” Solomon said, though he came no nearer. “I’d gladly sit up with you tonight, and Jane too. You could speak whenever you felt ready, or let me speak.”
“Yes, I’ll choose my own time. You needn’t offer me yours,” Peter replied.

“You can’t choose your time to die, though, Brother,” Mrs. Waule began in her usual muffled voice. “And when you can’t speak, you may grow tired of strangers around you. You may think of me and my children.” Her voice broke at the touching thought she was assigning to her speechless brother. References to ourselves naturally move us.
“No, I won’t,” the old man contradicted her. “I won’t think of any of you. I’ve made my will, I tell you. It’s made.” He turned toward Mrs. Vincy and swallowed more cordial.
“Some people would be ashamed to take a place that rightfully belongs to others,” Mrs. Waule said, directing her narrow eyes the same way.
“Ah, Sister,” Solomon replied with soft irony, “you and I aren’t fashionable, handsome, or clever enough. We must be humble and let the smart people push ahead of us.”
Fred could not endure that. Standing and looking at Featherstone, he asked, “Would you like Mother and me to go, sir, so you can be alone with your friends?”

“Sit down, I tell you,” Featherstone snapped. “Stay where you are. Goodbye, Solomon.” He tried to brandish his stick again, but with the handle reversed he could no longer manage it. “Goodbye, Mrs. Waule. Don’t come back.”
“I’ll be downstairs, Brother, whatever you say,” Solomon answered. “I’ll do my duty. We’ll see what the Almighty permits.”

“Yes, where property passing out of families is concerned,” Mrs. Waule added. “Especially with steady young men ready to carry on. I pity the ones who aren’t steady, and I pity their mothers. Goodbye, Brother Peter.”

“Remember, I’m next eldest after you, Brother. I prospered from the start just as you did, and there’s land in the Featherstone name already through me,” Solomon said. He placed considerable faith in this reflection, which might recur to Peter during the night. “For the present, then, goodbye.”
They hurried their departure when they saw Featherstone tug both sides of his wig, shut his eyes, and stretch his mouth in a grimace, as though determined to become both deaf and blind.

Nevertheless, they came daily and sat downstairs at their post of duty. Sometimes they exchanged low remarks so slowly that an observer might have imagined two speaking machines, with the mechanism’s success still in doubt: would it function, or spend a long time winding itself up only to stick and remain silent? Solomon and Jane would have regretted being quick. Brother Jonah, on the other side of the wall, showed what that led to.

Visitors from nearby and farther away sometimes varied their watch in the paneled parlor. With Peter upstairs, his property could be discussed in the light of all the local knowledge available on the spot. Several country and Middlemarch neighbors agreed strongly with the family and supported their claims against the Vincys. Some women even wept while talking to Mrs. Waule, recalling their own past disappointments through additions to wills or spiteful marriages made by ungrateful elderly gentlemen who might have been expected to survive for a better purpose. Such conversations stopped abruptly when Mary entered, like an organ whose bellows suddenly fall idle. Every eye turned toward her as a possible beneficiary, or someone who might gain access to locked iron chests.

The younger men among the relations and family connections, however, found this uncertainty attractive. They saw a capable girl who, among all the possibilities in the air, might prove at least a modest prize. Mary therefore received her share of compliments and courteous attentions.

Chief among those paying them was Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, a distinguished local bachelor and auctioneer who handled many sales of land and cattle. He was a public figure, his name appearing on widely distributed posters, and might reasonably feel sorry for anyone who had never heard of him. A second cousin of Peter Featherstone’s, he had been more agreeably treated than the other relations because he was useful in business. The old man had named him a pallbearer in the funeral arrangements he had dictated himself. There was no ugly greed in Mr. Trumbull, only an honest appreciation of his own merits, which he knew might count against rivals if there were competition. If Peter Featherstone, who had behaved toward him as well as any living soul could, should have made him a handsome bequest, he could only say he had never angled for favor or flattered. He had merely given advice drawn from his experience: twenty years of it, beginning with his apprenticeship at fifteen, and likely to have produced knowledge of no underhand sort. His admiration was not confined to himself. Both privately and professionally, he enjoyed placing high values on things. He delighted in elevated phrases and never used an inferior expression without immediately correcting it. This was fortunate, since he spoke loudly and tended to dominate a room. He frequently stood or walked about, tugging down his waistcoat with the air of a man who strongly agreed with himself, rapidly straightening his appearance with a forefinger, and marking each fresh sequence of movements by busily handling his large watch seals. A certain fierceness sometimes entered his manner, but it was mostly directed at mistaken opinions. There are so many of those to correct that a man with reading and experience must naturally have his patience tried. He considered the Featherstones generally limited in understanding, but as a worldly man and public figure he took them as he found them. He even went to converse with Jonah and young Cranch in the kitchen, certain that his searching questions about the Chalky Flats had greatly impressed the latter. If anyone had remarked that an auctioneer had to understand the nature of everything, Mr. Trumbull would have smiled and silently adjusted his appearance, feeling that he came close to it. On the whole, in the auctioneering line, he was honorable and unashamed of his business. He believed that “the celebrated Peel, now Sir Robert,” if introduced to him, would certainly recognize his importance.

“I wouldn’t object to a slice of that ham and a glass of that ale, Miss Garth, if you’ll permit me,” he said, entering the parlor at half past eleven. He had enjoyed the rare privilege of seeing Featherstone and now stood with his back to the fire between Solomon and Mrs. Waule.
“No need for you to leave the room. Allow me to ring.”
“Thank you, but I have something to do,” Mary answered.
“Well, Mr. Trumbull, you’re certainly a favorite,” Mrs. Waule observed.
“What, because I’ve seen the old gentleman?” The auctioneer handled his seals impartially. “Yes, well, he’s relied on me a good deal.” He pressed his lips together and frowned thoughtfully.
“May a man ask what his own brother has been saying?” Solomon inquired in a softly humble voice. Being rich and under no necessity to humble himself, he enjoyed the luxurious cunning of it.

“Certainly anyone may ask,” Mr. Trumbull replied with loud, good-natured but cutting sarcasm. “Anyone may interrogate. Anyone may give his observations an interrogative form.” His voice grew more resonant as his language rose. “Good speakers do it constantly, even when they expect no reply. We call it a figure of speech—speech at a high figure, one might say.” The eloquent auctioneer smiled at his own cleverness.
“I wouldn’t be sorry to hear he’d remembered you, Mr. Trumbull,” Solomon said. “I’ve never objected to deserving people. It’s the undeserving I object to.”

“Ah, that’s the point, you see. Precisely the point,” Mr. Trumbull said meaningfully. “There’s no denying that undeserving people have received legacies—even the residue of estates. Such things happen with testamentary dispositions.” Again he pursed his lips and frowned a little.
“Are you saying you know my brother has left his land outside the family, Mr. Trumbull?” Mrs. Waule asked. Not naturally hopeful, she found those long words depressing.
“He might as well hand the land straight to a charity as leave it to certain people,” Solomon remarked when his sister’s question received no answer.
“What, to a Blue-Coat charity school?” Mrs. Waule asked again. “Oh, Mr. Trumbull, surely you don’t mean that! It would defy the Almighty who made him prosper.”

While she spoke, Trumbull strolled from the hearth toward the window. His forefinger patrolled the inside of his neckcloth, then his whiskers and the curves of his hair. He moved to Miss Garth’s worktable, opened a book lying there, and read the title with the pompous emphasis of an auction announcement.

“‘Anne of Geierstein’”—he pronounced it “Jeersteen”—“‘or the Maiden of the Mist, by the author of Waverley.’” Turning the page, he began in a sonorous voice: “Almost four centuries have passed since the events described in the following chapters occurred on the Continent.” He placed the stress on the last syllable of that excellent final word. It was not ignorance of ordinary usage: he felt his novel pronunciation enhanced the rich sound he had given the whole passage.

Just then the servant arrived with the tray, safely carrying the moment for answering Mrs. Waule past. She and Solomon had watched his movements with the feeling that advanced learning sadly obstructed serious business. In truth, Mr. Trumbull knew nothing about the will. Short of being arrested for concealing treason, however, he could hardly have been made to admit ignorance of anything.

“Only a mouthful of ham and a glass of ale,” he said reassuringly. “A man with public duties must eat when he can. I’d back this ham against any in the three kingdoms,” he added after swallowing several bites at alarming speed. “Better than the hams at Freshitt Hall, in my judgment—and I consider myself a reasonably good judge.”
“Some people don’t care for so much sugar in a ham,” Mrs. Waule said. “My poor brother always insisted on it.”

“If anyone wants something better, they’re welcome to ask. But bless my soul, what a fragrance! I’d be glad to buy that quality. A gentleman feels a certain satisfaction”—his voice took on an emotional protest—“when a ham like this appears on his table.”

He pushed away his plate, poured himself ale, and drew his chair forward a little. The movement gave him a chance to inspect the insides of his legs, which he stroked approvingly. Mr. Trumbull possessed all those less frivolous gestures and mannerisms that distinguish the dominant peoples of the north.

“I see you have an interesting volume, Miss Garth,” he remarked when Mary returned. “By the author of ‘Waverley,’ which means Sir Walter Scott. I’ve bought one of his books myself: a very fine thing, an extremely superior publication, called ‘Ivanhoe.’ You won’t soon find a writer to beat him, I think—or, in my opinion, he will not speedily be surpassed. I’ve just read a passage at the commencement of ‘Anne of Jeersteen.’ It commences well.” Nothing ever began for Mr. Trumbull: in conversation as on his sale notices, it always commenced. “You’re fond of reading, evidently. Do you subscribe to the Middlemarch library?”
“No,” Mary replied. “Mr. Fred Vincy brought me this.”

“I’m quite a bookman myself,” Trumbull continued. “No fewer than two hundred volumes bound in calfskin, and well chosen, I flatter myself. Pictures too, by Murillo, Rubens, Teniers, Titian, Vandyck, and others. I’d gladly lend you any volume you cared to name, Miss Garth.”
“Thank you very much,” said Mary, hurrying off again, “but I have little time to read.”
“I’d say my brother has provided for her in his will,” Solomon murmured once the door closed, nodding toward the absent Mary.
“His first wife wasn’t much of a match for him,” Mrs. Waule said. “She brought no money. And this girl is only her niece—and a very proud girl too. My brother has always paid her wages.”

“A sensible young woman, in my opinion,” said Trumbull, draining his ale and rising with a forceful adjustment of his waistcoat. “I’ve watched her measure medicine by the drop. She pays attention to her task, sir. A great advantage in a woman, and for our friend upstairs, poor dear old soul. A man whose life has value ought to consider his wife as a nurse. That’s what I’d do if I married, and I believe I’ve been single long enough to avoid mistakes in that direction. Some men need marriage to raise them a little. If I ever need that, I hope someone will tell me—I hope some individual will inform me of the fact. Good morning, Mrs. Waule. Good morning, Mr. Solomon. I trust our next meeting will take place under less sorrowful circumstances.”
After Trumbull left with an impressive bow, Solomon leaned toward his sister. “Depend on it, Jane, my brother has left that girl a great lump of money.”
“You’d certainly think so from Mr. Trumbull’s manner,” Jane replied. After a pause she added, “He talks as though my daughters couldn’t be trusted to measure drops.”
“Auctioneers talk extravagantly,” Solomon said. “Though Trumbull has certainly made money.”

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: Shortly after midnight Mary Garth took over the watch in Mr. Featherstone’s room and remained alone with him through the early hours. She often chose this duty and found some pleasure in it, despite his irritability whenever he needed her. Between his demands she could sit completely still, enjoying the surrounding quiet and the dim light. The red fire, with its soft sounds of movement, seemed a solemn form of life, serenely independent of the petty passions, foolish desires, and pursuit of worthless uncertainties that daily provoked her contempt. Mary enjoyed her own thoughts and could entertain herself well in the half-light with her hands in her lap. She had learned early, and for compelling reasons, that the world was unlikely to arrange itself for her particular satisfaction. She wasted no time being astonished or offended by the fact. Already she largely regarded life as a comedy in which she had proudly—even generously—resolved never to play the mean or treacherous part. She might have grown cynical without parents she respected and a deep reserve of loving gratitude, made fuller by her refusal to expect too much.

Tonight, as usual, she turned over the day’s scenes. Her lips often curled in amusement at oddities her imagination made funnier still. People and their illusions were so absurd: wearing fools’ caps without knowing it, imagining their own lies opaque while everyone else’s were transparent, exempting themselves from every rule, as though a lamp that made the whole world yellow left them alone rosy. Yet some illusions she witnessed did not seem entirely comic. With no evidence beyond her close study of Featherstone’s character, she privately believed the Vincys were as likely to be disappointed as the relations he kept away, however much he liked having them around. She felt considerable contempt for Mrs. Vincy’s obvious fear of leaving her alone with Fred. Even so, she worried about how Fred would bear it if his uncle left him as poor as before. In his presence she could make him the target of a joke; in his absence his foolishness gave her no pleasure.

Still, she enjoyed thinking. A vigorous young mind not overwhelmed by passion finds satisfaction in learning about life and takes an interested view of its own developing powers. Mary had plenty of laughter inside her.

No solemnity or sorrow for the old man in the bed ran through these reflections. Such emotions are easier to pretend than to feel toward someone whose remaining life seems to consist only of surviving vices. Mary had always known Featherstone at his least pleasant. He took no pride in her; she was merely useful. Concern for a soul that constantly snaps at you must be left to earthly saints, and Mary was no saint. She had never answered him harshly and had served him faithfully. That was as far as she could go. Featherstone himself felt no concern for his soul and had refused to discuss it with Mr. Tucker.

Tonight he had not snapped at her. For the first hour or two he lay unusually still. At last she heard his bunch of keys rattle against the tin box he always kept beside him in bed. Around three o’clock he said with striking clarity, “Come here, missy!”

Mary went to him. He had already pulled the box from under the bedclothes, though he generally asked her to do it, and had chosen the key. Unlocking it, he took out another key and looked directly at her. His eyes seemed to have regained all their sharpness. “How many of them are in the house?”
“You mean your own relations, sir?” Mary asked, familiar with his way of speaking. He gave a slight nod, and she continued.
“Mr. Jonah Featherstone and young Cranch are staying overnight.”
“Ah, so they’re sticking, are they? And the others come every day, I suppose—Solomon, Jane, all the youngsters? Peeping about, counting up, doing their sums?”
“They don’t all come daily. Mr. Solomon and Mrs. Waule do, and the others visit often.”

He listened with a grimace, then relaxed his face. “More fools them. Listen, missy. It’s three in the morning, and my mind’s as clear as it ever was. I know every bit of my property, where the money’s invested, everything. I’ve arranged it all so I can change my mind and please myself at the end. Do you hear? I have all my faculties.”
“Yes, sir?” Mary answered calmly.

He lowered his voice, looking more cunning still. “I’ve made two wills, and I mean to burn one. Do exactly what I say. This key opens the iron chest in that cupboard. Push hard beside the brass plate at the top until it slides like a bolt. Then put the key in the front lock and turn it. Go and do it. Take the top paper out. ‘Last Will and Testament,’ printed large.”
“No, sir,” Mary said firmly. “I can’t do that.”
“Can’t? I’m telling you that you must.” His voice began to tremble at the shock of resistance.
“I can’t touch your chest or your will. I have to refuse anything that could expose me to suspicion.”
“I tell you, I’m perfectly sane. Am I not to do what I choose at the end? I made two wills for this very reason. Take the key.”
“No, sir. I won’t,” Mary answered with greater firmness. Her aversion was growing.
“There’s no time to waste, I tell you.”
“I can’t help that, sir. I won’t let the end of your life stain the beginning of mine. I will not touch the chest or your will.” She stepped back from the bed.
He stared blankly for a while, holding the single key upright on its ring. Then, with an agitated jerk, he began using his bony left hand to empty the tin box in front of him.
“Missy,” he said hurriedly, “look! Take the money, the banknotes and the gold. Here, take it! You can have the lot. Just do as I say.”
He strained to reach the key toward her. Mary stepped farther away.
“I won’t touch either the key or the money, sir. Please don’t ask again. If you do, I’ll have to fetch your brother.”

His hand fell. For the first time Mary saw Peter Featherstone cry like a child. “Please put your money away, sir,” she said as gently as she could. Then she returned to her chair beside the fire, hoping to show him that further demands would be useless. After a while he recovered himself and spoke eagerly.
“Then listen. Fetch the young fellow. Fetch Fred Vincy.”
Mary’s heart quickened. Possibilities rushed through her mind about what destroying a second will might mean. She had to make a difficult choice at once.
“I’ll fetch him if you let me bring Mr. Jonah and some others too.”
“No one else. Just the young fellow. I’ll do what I please.”
“Wait until daylight, sir, when everyone’s up. Or shall I call Simmons now and send him for the lawyer? He could be here within two hours.”
“The lawyer? What do I want him for? No one is to know. No one, I tell you. I’ll do as I please.”

“Please let me bring someone else, sir,” Mary urged. She felt uncomfortable alone with him. A strange flare of nervous energy seemed to let him speak repeatedly without breaking into his usual cough. Yet she did not want to upset him further by opposing him unnecessarily. “Please let me call somebody.”
“Leave me alone, I say. Look, missy, take the money. You’ll never get another chance. Nearly two hundred, and there’s more in the box. Nobody knows how much was here. Take it and do what I tell you.”

Standing by the fire, Mary watched its red light fall on the old man, propped against his pillows and bedrest, his skeletal hand extending the key and the money spread on the quilt. She never forgot that picture of a man determined to have his own way at the end. But the manner of his offer made her refusal harder and more resolute than ever.
“It’s useless, sir. I won’t do it. Put the money away. I won’t touch it. I’ll do anything else I can to make you comfortable, but I will not touch your keys or your money.”
“Anything else! Anything else!” he rasped furiously. As in a nightmare, he struggled to shout but could scarcely be heard. “I want nothing else. Come here. Come here!”

Knowing him too well, Mary approached cautiously. He dropped his keys and tried to seize the walking stick, staring at her like an old hyena. The effort in his hand twisted the muscles of his face. She stopped beyond his reach.
“Let me give you a little cordial,” she said quietly. “Try to calm yourself. Perhaps you’ll sleep. Tomorrow, when it’s light, you can do what you want.”

Although she was out of range, he lifted the stick and threw it with a violent effort that achieved nothing. It slipped over the foot of the bed and fell. Mary left it there and went back to the fireside. She would bring the cordial later; exhaustion would quiet him. The coldest hour of the morning was approaching. The fire had burned low, and through the gap in the heavy woolen curtains she could see the pale light filtered by the blind. She added wood to the fire, wrapped herself in a shawl, and sat down, hoping he would sleep now. Going near him might only prolong his irritation. He had said nothing since throwing the stick, though she had watched him pick up his keys again and rest his right hand on the money. He did not put it away, and she thought he was falling asleep.
Now, however, the memory of what had happened troubled Mary more than the event itself. She began to question decisions that had felt imperative at the critical moment and had left no room for doubt.

The dry wood suddenly flared, lighting every corner. She saw him lying still, his head turned slightly aside. She approached without a sound. His face seemed strangely motionless, but then the shifting firelight made everything appear to move, and she was unsure. Her heart beat so violently that she distrusted her senses. Even after touching him and listening for his breath, she could not trust her conclusion. She went to the window and gently held back the curtain and blind, letting the steady light of the sky fall across the bed.

A moment later she rushed to the bell and rang hard. Very soon there was no doubt: Peter Featherstone was dead, his right hand gripping the keys and his left resting on the pile of banknotes and gold.
